final_answer:
Short answer: Probably no on both. Client likely cannot lawfully stop paying Lessor, and Lessor is likely not responsible for the defective Trailers. Client's remedy runs against Manufacturer, mainly through its bankruptcy claim. CAVEAT: every primary-source fetch (Virginia Code and uniform UCC text) was blocked by the network proxy, so none of the following is source-verified in this run. It rests on my recall of Virginia's Article 2A and on one search-result summary that I did not treat as authority. No citation is offered under the firewall.

1. Finance lease. Under Va. Code Title 8.2A (UCC Article 2A), a 'finance lease' exists when (i) the lessor does not select, manufacture or supply the goods; (ii) the lessor acquires the goods in connection with the lease; and (iii) the lessee receives the supply contract (or its approved equivalent) before signing the lease. Here Client chose the model and negotiated the specs with Manufacturer. Lessor only financed the purchase and bought the Trailers for the lease. Lessor also gave Client the full purchase agreement before signing. These facts fit the definition. Client is a business, so this is not a consumer lease.

2. Payment obligation. Section 8.2A-407 makes the lessee's promises under a non-consumer finance lease irrevocable and independent once the lessee accepts the goods. The 'absolute and unconditional' clause adds contractual emphasis, and the statute makes it self-executing. The promises are enforceable against Client and Lessor's assignees, and Client cannot cancel, terminate or excuse them without Lessor's consent. Accordingly, the compressor failures and Manufacturer's bankruptcy do not by themselves excuse Client's rent. Stopping payment would be a lease default, exposing Client to Lessor's default remedies. These include accelerating or recovering the rent, repossessing the Trailers, and possibly attorney's fees if the Lease provides for them. Client should not withhold payments on the strength of the defects.

3. Lessor's responsibility. In a finance lease, the lessor generally gives no implied warranties of merchantability or fitness. Section 8.2A-209 instead gives the lessee the benefit of the supplier's promises and warranties, express and implied, under the supply contract. This includes the two-year warranty. The Lease also disclaims Lessor's warranties and directs equipment claims to Manufacturer. Nothing in the facts shows Lessor selected or supplied the goods, or made its own warranty or misrepresentation. So Lessor is not liable for the defects.

4. Caveats. (a) Client's rights run against Manufacturer: file a proof of claim in the Chapter 7 case for breach of warranty and the repair costs, and check for any assigned warranty, third-party warranty or service obligor, and any insurance. Recovery as an unsecured creditor may be small. (b) The Lease's disclaimers must be conspicuous and in writing, which I could not verify. (c) Exceptions could change the outcome: Lessor's own fraud, misrepresentation or active concealment; Lessor's own undertakings to Client; Lessor's own breach (for example, an assurance of performance); unconscionability; and any Lease-specific carve-outs. A Virginia decision applying 8.2A-407 to these facts was not reviewed. (d) Whether the clause is also valid as a waiver of defenses depends on the Lease terms, which were not provided. (e) Client might negotiate a restructuring, repair or replacement with Lessor, but Lessor has no obligation to agree.
